issues.legal_issue: A landlord occupying a rented non-residential building, without an absolute right to possess it, is not thereby barred from seeking possession of another non-residential building for a bona fide business need.
material_facts: The landlord sought possession of a non-residential building to move a business he was carrying on in a rented building.
The trial court and the appellate court found that the landlord bona fide required the disputed building for that business.
The appellate court held that the landlord could not obtain possession unless he was prepared to vacate the rented building; the High Court set that order aside.
issues.conclusion: The landlord’s occupation of the rented building did not make him ‘entitled to possession’ of it for the purpose of the statutory restriction, and the eviction order was properly restored.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 8(3)(a)(ii) of the Mysore House Rent and Accommodation Control Act, 1951, a landlord seeking a non-residential building for a business must not already be in occupation of a non-residential building owned by, or one to the possession of which the landlord is entitled. A tenant who may remain in possession only until a ground for eviction under section 8(2) is established has statutory immunity from eviction, not the positive entitlement to possession contemplated by section 8(3)(a)(ii). The Court approved S. G. Narayanappa and Bros. v. A. N. Narasimhiah, [1962] Mys. L.J. 760, and the reasoning in Kai Khushrao v. Bai Jerbai, A.I.R. 1949 F.C. 124; it overruled V. Thanappa Chetty v. Arcot Govindaswami Naicker, A.I.R. 1952 Mad. 553.

rule.if: nonresidential_eviction_application and bona_fide_business_need and landlord_occupies_rented_business_premises and landlord_lacks_absolute_possession_right

predicates.nonresidential_eviction_application: A landlord applied to recover a non-residential building from a tenant.
predicates.bona_fide_business_need: The landlord genuinely needed the building for a business the landlord was carrying on.
predicates.landlord_occupies_rented_business_premis: The landlord carried on the business from another non-residential building occupied as a tenant.
predicates.landlord_lacks_absolute_possession_right: The landlord could remain in the other building only while no prescribed ground for eviction was established.

issues.definition: When a landlord genuinely needs a non-residential building for a business and occupies another business building only as a tenant without an absolute right to possess it, the landlord is not barred from seeking eviction on that ground.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court may set aside an appellate order in statutory revision when the appellate court materially irregularly fails to follow an applicable High Court decision.
material_facts: The matter came before the High Court in a revision under section 17 of the Act against an appellate order concerning eviction.
The appellate court’s decision conflicted with an applicable decision of the High Court, given in a case arising from an earlier order of that same appellate judge.
The High Court found that the failure to follow its decision amounted to material irregularity and set aside the appellate order.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was entitled to set aside the appellate order in revision; its intervention was not shown to be improper.
issues.legal_principle: Although the High Court’s jurisdiction under section 17 of the Mysore House Rent and Accommodation Control Act, 1951, is limited, an appellate court’s failure to follow an applicable High Court decision may constitute material irregularity warranting revision. The Supreme Court found no basis under Article 136 of the Constitution to hold that the High Court should not have intervened.

predicates.statutory_revision_proceeding: A party challenged an appellate order before the High Court through a statutory revision proceeding.
predicates.subordinate_appellate_court_disregarded_: The appellate court did not follow an applicable decision of the High Court.
predicates.disregard_amounted_to_material_irregular: The failure to follow that decision constituted a material irregularity in the appellate court’s decision.

issues.definition: In a statutory revision proceeding, when an appellate court disregards an applicable High Court decision and that disregard amounts to material irregularity, the High Court may set aside the appellate order.
